story.title: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk

facts.text: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.
Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac.
Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Apple is making it harder for apps to get sweeping access to a Mac.

It did point to AI agents, though, warning that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more capable and autonomous.AI agents on the Mac now routinely ask for full system accessThe announcement follows a claim by US columnist Jason Aten that Meta's Muse AI agent read private messages on his Mac mini without his permission.

"Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk," Apple wrote, adding that this happens without users' "full knowledge and understanding".Apple also flagged a less obvious concern.
In a post on its developer website, Apple said the setting exists so backup apps can work properly, and that it largely bypasses the privacy controls built into macOS.
Apple's aim is to make sure anyone handing an AI agent that much control knows what they are signing off on.You use AI every day.
Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.
